appTagline: Analyze blood type genetics and transfusion compatibility

step1.title: 1. Provide Inputs
step1.desc: Enter the known blood types for the father, mother, and any children or if you don't know a person's blood type, you can leave it unknown to see probabilities. If you want the calculations for only one type of blood type (e.g., ABO only), leave the other blood type entries (i.e., RH) completely unknown; Use either phenotypes (like A+) or genotypes (like AO/Dd).

step2.title: 2. Calculate Odds
step2.desc: We cross-reference all valid genetic combinations to calculate the precise probability of each possible blood type for every member. For example, you may not have any information about one or more individuals and you want to obtain complete information about them, or you may know the phenotype of an individual and you want to see what their genotype is.
step2.note: Note: Calculations are based on standard Mendelian inheritance and do not account for rare mutations or other genetic exceptions.

step3.title: 3. Understand Transfusions
step3.desc: This analysis also shows who can donate blood to whom. Now, you may know the blood types of a person or people and then see who this person can donate blood to and also from whom they can receive blood, or you may not know the blood type of the person or people and want to see what the probabilities are for them to donate and receive blood.

punnett.title: Example: Punnett Square
punnett.desc: This tool helps visualize how parents' alleles combine. For instance, if a child has Type O blood, they must have inherited an 'O' allele from each parent. Therefore, a Type 'A' parent of a Type 'O' child must have the genotype AO, not AA.

transfusionDiagram.title: Transfusion Rules Example
transfusionDiagram.desc: A person with Type A blood has 'A' antigens on their red blood cells. Their immune system will attack 'B' antigens. Therefore, they can donate to other 'A' types and 'AB' types (who have both antigens), but not 'B' or 'O' types.
transfusionDiagram.rhNote: Note: Rh-negative blood can be given to Rh-positive recipients, but not vice-versa.

examples.genoToPheno: AO shows up as blood type A, because A is dominant over O.
examples.rhInheritance: Dd with Dd gives DD (25%), Dd (50%), and dd (25%).
examples.dAlleleDominance: Dd shows up as Rh+, because D is dominant.
examples.mendelianInheritance: AO with BO gives AB, A, B, and O, each with a 25% chance.
examples.genoProbability: 25 AA results out of 100 combinations means the chance of AA is 0.25.
examples.phenoProbability: Chance of type A is the chance of AA plus the chance of AO: 0.25 + 0.50 = 0.75.
examples.normalization: Scores 0.30, 0.60, and 0.20 add up to 1.10, so they scale to about 0.27, 0.55, and 0.18.
examples.hybridProbability: Chance of A+ is the chance of A times the chance of Rh+: 0.40 × 0.85 = 0.34.
examples.comboValidity: Parents AA and BB cannot have an O child, so that case is rejected.
examples.transfusion: Someone who is A+ or A- can always receive O- blood.
examples.cartesian: Four ABO groups times two Rh factors gives eight blood types, from A+ to O-.
